issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Ravi Patel is a 64-year-old warehouse worker who came to treatment after months of worsening nights, saying that darkness now feels less like the end of the day than the beginning of something dangerous. He is married and has spent years on steady physical work, unloading shipments and moving pallets in a large distribution warehouse on the outskirts of town. He described the traumatic event as a period of captivity that began during an evening shift, at almost the same hour that still troubles him now. He had been finishing work when he was forcibly confined by others and kept overnight in a dark enclosed space. What stands out in his account is not elaboration but the sensory precision of what remains with him: the darkness, the helpless waiting, and the repeated awareness that he could not get out or protect himself. At one point during that captivity, he became acutely aware of snakes nearby, or believed they were nearby, and since then even casual conversation about snakes or a photograph of one is enough to make his whole body tense. He still speaks about that time carefully, as if getting too close to the memory might undo him. He has come to believe that if he lets himself think about it fully, he will not be able to handle what comes up.

In the weeks after the event, Ravi noticed that the approach of the same time of day brought a shift in him even when nothing was happening around him. Late afternoon moving toward evening became charged. At work, as the light outside the warehouse bay doors started to fade, he would find himself scanning the floor behind him and turning suddenly to check whether anyone was there. The warehouse itself, with its dim aisles and shadowed corners, became hard to tolerate once daylight dropped. He stayed on edge through the last part of his shift, certain he needed to remain superalert. When coworkers walked up behind him unexpectedly, he would jerk around before he even knew he was doing it. He did not explain much to them. He only knew that his body behaved as if danger was close and could come from behind.

Night became the hardest part of the day. Ravi reported that he finds it much harder to feel safe at night than during daylight, and this has shaped his routine at home. He delays going to bed for as long as he can, lingering in the living room with lights on, dozing in a chair rather than lying down in the dark. Waking in darkness is especially difficult; when he opens his eyes and the room is black, he is immediately alert, checking his body for signs that something is wrong, running his hands over himself, noticing every ache or sensation as if it might mean injury or danger. He has also begun repeatedly asking his wife to tell him he is okay. Sometimes he asks directly whether the doors are locked, whether everything is fine, whether he seems normal. The reassurance helps only briefly, and he often asks again. His wife has become worried and worn down, especially because neither of them is sleeping well anymore.

Over time, Ravi’s world has narrowed around these habits. He avoids lying in the dark, avoids images or talk of snakes, and avoids letting his mind settle on what happened. He is not dismissive about the event; rather, he seems frightened by the possibility of remembering too much. What frightened him most in session was not only the event itself but the sense that it proved something unbearable: that bad things can happen to him and he cannot stop them. He said this with the flat certainty of someone who no longer experiences safety as dependable. Alongside that, he admitted with difficulty that there are times he is not sure his life is worth living anymore. He did not describe a wish to die so much as a bleakness about whether life can feel livable again if every evening turns into a period of watchfulness.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a recent stretch of nights when he had hardly slept and began dreading the end of each workday. One evening in the warehouse, as the shift moved toward closing time, a coworker joked about finding a snake in a shipment, and Ravi felt himself go cold and immediately looked behind him, then around the loading area, as if he had been transported back to that enclosed darkness. He went home shaken, stayed awake most of the night, and kept asking his wife to reassure him that he was safe. By the time he came for treatment, he was exhausted and discouraged. He said he wants help because he cannot keep living with every night feeling dangerous, but he is also afraid that talking about what happened will make it all come back in a way he will not be able to bear.
